title: AD-integrated DNS and Domain Controller Location
summary: Understand why DNS is a dependency of AD DS, how clients locate domain controllers, and why DNS faults frequently surface as authentication or replication incidents.
objective: Explain the DNS dependency chain behind DC discovery and replication, then identify the DNS layer to inspect before changing AD objects or topology.
body_outline: AD DS uses DNS so clients can locate domain controllers and so domain controllers can locate one another for directory operations and replication.
Active Directory-integrated DNS zones store zone data in AD DS and replicate it through directory replication rather than traditional secondary-zone transfers.

When authentication, Group Policy, or replication fails, validate client DNS configuration, authoritative zone data, DC registrations, delegation and name resolution before treating the symptom as an AD database fault.
Use evidence from DNS lookups and DC-locator tests to separate name-resolution failure from network, Kerberos, LDAP, or replication-engine failure.
quick_check: Why can a DNS problem present as both a logon problem and an AD replication problem?

title: AD DNS in Plain English: The Directory's Address Book
summary: Active Directory depends on DNS to find the right domain controller and the services running on it.
analogy: Think of AD as a company with many specialist desks. DNS is the internal directory that tells a client which desk handles logon, LDAP, Kerberos or global-catalog requests. If the directory points to the wrong place, the service can be healthy but still look unavailable.
plain_language_explanation: Domain-joined systems must use DNS information that can resolve the AD namespace and discover domain controllers. Before rebuilding accounts, resetting secure channels or changing replication settings, first prove that DNS is returning the expected AD records.
visual_hint: Show a client querying DNS, receiving a DC service record, then contacting the selected domain controller.
quick_check: If a domain client uses a public DNS resolver instead of the AD DNS service, what kind of failure would you investigate first?

title: DNS, DC Locator and Replication Dependency Mapping
summary: Trace the dependency path from client resolver configuration through AD DNS records to domain-controller selection and directory replication.
architecture_notes: AD DNS design and AD site topology are coupled operationally: DNS enables service discovery while sites and subnets influence locality and the domain controller a client should prefer.
internals: A healthy AD namespace must let clients and DCs resolve the directory's service records and host records consistently. Directory-integrated zones reduce separate zone-transfer administration by using AD replication for the zone data itself.
failure_modes: Common anti-patterns include clients pointing only to non-AD resolvers, stale or missing DC registrations, incorrect delegation, and site/subnet definitions that cause clients to select non-local domain controllers.
trade_offs: Centralizing DNS forwarding and policy can simplify governance, but AD clients still require reliable access to DNS servers that can resolve the AD namespace and its service-discovery records.
enterprise_design_notes: Treat DNS health, AD site design, authentication, and replication as one dependency graph during incident response instead of troubleshooting each technology in isolation.

title: Read-only AD DNS and DC Locator Health Check
summary: Validate AD service discovery using non-destructive DNS and domain-controller location checks before making any configuration change.
objective: Collect enough read-only evidence to decide whether a domain-join, logon or replication symptom is caused by DNS/DC discovery rather than changing AD configuration prematurely.
prerequisites_detail: A domain-joined Windows lab client with standard command-line tools and permission to read DNS and domain information.
environment: One domain-joined client and at least one reachable domain controller in a lab or controlled test domain.
topology: Client -> configured DNS resolver -> AD DNS namespace -> selected domain controller.
steps: Record the client's configured DNS servers with `ipconfig /all`; verify they are the intended enterprise resolvers for the AD namespace.
Resolve the AD domain and known domain-controller hostnames with `nslookup` or `Resolve-DnsName` and record the returned servers and addresses.
Query a domain-controller service record such as `_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<domain>` and confirm at least one expected DC is returned.
Run `nltest /dsgetdc:<domain> /force` and record the selected DC and site information.
Compare the selected DC with the expected site/subnet design; if unexpected, escalate to site/subnet and DNS-registration review rather than altering client trust state.
expected_result: The client uses an approved resolver, AD service records resolve, and DC Locator returns a reachable domain controller consistent with the intended site design.
validation: Repeat the checks from a second client or subnet to distinguish a local resolver/client issue from an authoritative-zone or site-wide issue.
rollback: Not required; the exercise is read-only.
cleanup: Store only non-sensitive diagnostic evidence and remove temporary notes containing internal hostnames if your lab handling policy requires it.

title: Domain Logon or Replication Fails Because AD DNS Discovery Is Wrong
summary: Use a bounded decision tree to separate client DNS configuration, service-record registration, authoritative-zone data, site selection and general connectivity failures.
symptoms: Domain logon is slow or fails
A client cannot locate a domain controller
Group Policy processing reports DC/name-resolution errors
Replication diagnostics report name-resolution or partner-discovery failures
diagnostic_order: Confirm the affected system's DNS client configuration.
Resolve the AD domain and known DC hostnames.
Query the AD service records used for DC discovery.
Confirm DC Locator output and the client's detected AD site.
Only after DNS/DC discovery is proven healthy continue into network, Kerberos, LDAP, secure-channel or replication-engine troubleshooting.
escalation_boundary: Do not reset machine accounts, force metadata cleanup, change site links, or rebuild DNS zones merely because the symptom mentions Active Directory. Escalate only after the read-only evidence identifies the failing dependency.

title: Group Policy Architecture, Scope and Processing
summary: Understand the two-part GPO architecture, site/domain/OU scope, inheritance, and why policy-processing evidence should be collected before editing production GPOs.
objective: Explain where a GPO is stored, how scope is established, and how to reason about policy application without immediately editing the policy.
body_outline: A domain GPO has a Group Policy container in Active Directory and a Group Policy template in SYSVOL; both components must be available and consistent.
GPOs can be linked to sites, domains and OUs. The user's or computer's location in AD and GPO scope determine applicability.
Computer policy applies at startup and user policy at sign-in, with background refresh afterward.
Troubleshooting should distinguish scope, permissions, replication/SYSVOL availability and client-side extension processing before changing settings.
quick_check: Why can an AD replication or SYSVOL problem cause a Group Policy symptom even when the GPO itself was configured correctly?

title: Sites, Subnets and Replication Topology as an Operational Design
summary: Model physical network boundaries in AD so client queries and replication traffic follow intended locality and WAN-cost assumptions.
objective: Explain how sites, subnets, site links and site-link costs influence DC placement, client locality and replication behavior.
body_outline: An AD site topology is a logical representation of the physical network used to route directory queries and replication traffic efficiently.
Subnets map IP ranges to sites; missing or incorrect mappings can cause clients to select remote domain controllers.
Site links and their costs/schedules describe intended intersite replication paths and WAN preferences.
Topology changes should be based on network evidence and capacity/failure requirements, not used as a first-response workaround for unrelated replication errors.
quick_check: What operational symptom can appear when a branch-office subnet is not mapped to its correct AD site?

title: LDAP Signing, Channel Binding and Windows Server 2025 Security Defaults
summary: Understand the integrity protections around LDAP authentication and the stronger default posture documented for new Windows Server 2025 AD deployments.
objective: Explain LDAP signing and channel binding, identify Windows Server 2025 default-security implications, and plan compatibility validation before enforcing stronger policy in an existing estate.
body_outline: LDAP signing provides message integrity and authenticity; channel binding ties authentication to the underlying TLS session to resist session hijacking and man-in-the-middle attacks.
Microsoft documents stronger defaults for new Windows Server 2025 AD deployments, including LDAP signing required by default and channel binding set to When supported.
Existing applications and appliances can have LDAP compatibility dependencies, so enforcement changes in an established estate require discovery, event monitoring, testing and rollback planning.
AD hardening is broader than one policy: protect privileged groups, reduce standing privilege, use secure administrative hosts, patch critical infrastructure and maintain a recovery plan.
quick_check: Why should LDAP-signing enforcement in an existing enterprise be preceded by compatibility discovery instead of treated as a blind security toggle?

title: AD DNS, Group Policy, Sites and LDAP Security Checkpoint
summary: Scenario-based checkpoint covering the four new operational domains introduced in BATCH-020R3.

assessment_items.question: A branch client authenticates against a distant DC even though a local DC is healthy. Which configuration area should be checked before changing replication?
assessment_items.answer: Validate the client's subnet-to-site mapping and DNS/DC Locator results so the client is associated with the intended AD site.

assessment_items.question: A GPO exists in AD but clients cannot read its policy files. Which second GPO component and service dependency should be checked?
assessment_items.answer: Check the Group Policy template in SYSVOL and the health/availability of SYSVOL replication and access.

assessment_items.question: Why do LDAP signing and channel binding protect different layers?
assessment_items.answer: Signing protects LDAP message integrity/authenticity, while channel binding ties authentication to the TLS channel so the authenticated session cannot be transparently relayed onto another TLS connection.

assessment_items.question: What is the safe first action before tightening LDAP enforcement in an established estate?
assessment_items.answer: Inventory and monitor existing LDAP clients, test compatibility in a controlled environment, and prepare rollback/change control before enforcement.

title: Senior AD Engineer Scenarios: DNS, GPO, Sites and LDAP Security
summary: Senior-level interview scenarios that test dependency reasoning rather than memorized commands.

questions.question: Users in one site report slow logons after a network redesign. How do you triage without making a risky AD change?
answer_outline: Confirm affected subnets and client DNS settings
Validate subnet-to-site mapping and DC Locator output
Check selected DC reachability and DNS service records
Review replication only after locality/discovery is proven

questions.question: A security team asks you to require LDAP signing immediately on all DCs. What do you do?
answer_outline: Confirm current OS/domain scope and policy state
Inventory LDAP clients and monitor compatibility signals
Test enforcement in a representative non-production scope
Implement controlled rollout with rollback and owner approval

questions.question: Why can Group Policy failure be a replication problem rather than a policy-authoring problem?
answer_outline: A GPO has an AD component and a SYSVOL component
Both must be available and converged
Scope and client-side processing must also be validated before editing settings
